clinicalPearls: Consider in any hypertensive patient with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia, treatment-resistant hypertension, or an incidentally found adrenal mass
Most patients are normokalemic at presentation; hypokalemia is present in only a minority, so a normal potassium does not exclude the diagnosis
Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the preferred screening test and should be checked before starting mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists

Screening should target patients with sustained BP above standard thresholds, resistant hypertension, hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma, or hypertension with sleep apnea or a family history of early-onset hypertension/stroke
Unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia are the two dominant subtypes and require different management (surgery versus mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist)
Adrenal vein sampling is generally required to distinguish unilateral from bilateral disease before considering surgery, since imaging alone is unreliable in this regard

Correcting the underlying aldosterone excess improves blood pressure control and reduces the excess cardiovascular and renal risk associated with this condition beyond what is expected from hypertension alone
harrison.pathophysiology: Autonomous, renin-independent overproduction of aldosterone from one or both adrenal glands leads to sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, and volume-mediated hypertension. The excess mineralocorticoid activity suppresses plasma renin and can produce hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, though many patients remain normokalemic. Beyond hemodynamic effects, chronic aldosterone excess produces direct pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory effects on the heart, vasculature, and kidney that account for disproportionate target-organ damage relative to blood pressure alone.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia variants (11-beta-hydroxylase or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency)
nonInfectiousMimics: Licorice or chewing-tobacco-induced pseudohyperaldosteronism (apparent mineralocorticoid excess)
Diuretic-induced hypokalemia with secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism
Renal artery stenosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism
Chronic laxative abuse or bulimia causing hypokalemia
additionalInvestigations: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio — first-line screening test, best done after correcting hypokalemia and adjusting interfering medications
Confirmatory suppression testing (e.g., oral sodium loading, saline infusion, or fludrocortisone suppression) — establishes autonomous aldosterone secretion when screening is positive
Adrenal CT — identifies adrenal masses and helps exclude adrenocortical carcinoma, but cannot reliably lateralize functional source
Adrenal vein sampling — gold standard for lateralizing unilateral versus bilateral aldosterone hypersecretion prior to surgical decision-making
Serum potassium and bicarbonate — assess for hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, though normal values do not exclude disease
Plasma renin activity or direct renin concentration — confirms renin suppression characteristic of primary aldosteronism
Genetic testing — considered in early-onset hypertension or strong family history to evaluate for familial hyperaldosteronism syndromes
24-hour urinary aldosterone excretion — used as part of some confirmatory protocols
redFlags: Severe or refractory hypokalemia with muscle weakness, cramps, or cardiac arrhythmia
Resistant hypertension requiring three or more antihypertensive agents including a diuretic
Adrenal incidentaloma with hypertension or hypokalemia raising concern for functioning adenoma or carcinoma
Very young age of hypertension onset or hypertensive stroke in a young relative, suggesting a familial syndrome
Large or irregular adrenal mass on imaging raising concern for adrenocortical carcinoma
pitfalls: Failing to correct hypokalemia and withdraw interfering drugs (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, high-dose diuretics) before aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing, leading to false results
Relying on adrenal CT alone to decide unilateral versus bilateral disease instead of adrenal vein sampling, risking inappropriate or missed surgery
Assuming normokalemia excludes the diagnosis and therefore not screening appropriately hypertensive patients
Misattributing resistant hypertension to poor adherence or essential hypertension without screening for secondary causes
harrison.prognosis: With correct subtype classification, unilateral disease treated surgically often achieves cure or major improvement of hypertension and hypokalemia, while bilateral disease managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists generally achieves good blood pressure control. Untreated or unrecognized disease carries excess risk of cardiovascular events, stroke, and chronic kidney disease compared with blood-pressure-matched essential hypertension.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Disorders of the Adrenal Cortex (Primary Aldosteronism)
management: Lateralise the source with adrenal vein sampling, then treat a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma with laparoscopic adrenalectomy
Manage bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and non-surgical candidates medically with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone or eplerenone
Correct hypokalaemia and control blood pressure, with dietary sodium restriction, before and alongside definitive treatment
For glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, use low-dose glucocorticoid to suppress ACTH-driven aldosterone production
Monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renal function after adrenalectomy for cure, and track renin, potassium, and creatinine in those on receptor antagonists
Offer genetic testing and counselling for suspected familial hyperaldosteronism, particularly in young patients with a family history of early hypertension or stroke
